source.title: Unveiling the Hessian's Connection to the Decision Boundary
source.authors: Mahalakshmi Sabanayagam; Freya Behrens; U. Adomaityte; Anna Dawid

record.tranche_reason: The paper compares a new Hessian-gradient generalization measure with training/test generalization across deliberately different minima, using a different measurement method from the catalog versions.
record.gate_note: The paper tests whether its Hessian-based measure tracks generalization across minima. It does not test memorization capacity, the listed optimizer or batch-size comparisons, dropout, or removal of memorized examples. Alignment values used to construct the measure are not separate result rows. Rows record reported generalization-measure values and the margin comparison that bears on whether the measure tracks the gap.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates Hessian-gradient alignment, decision-boundary complexity and a proposed margin estimator. It does not measure V7's magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance or its correlation with train–test gaps. Unscaled Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue are different measures. None of V1–V8 is tested; optimizer alignment plots and random-label pretraining also do not establish the corresponding generalization claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors conclude that top Hessian eigenvectors encode decision-boundary information, propose Gθ as a promising complexity-based generalization measure, acknowledge failures involving simplicity bias and complexity far from training samples, and propose a margin estimator. Their reported comparisons do not provide numerical train–test gaps, and the real-data generalization ordering relies on the established interpretation of adversarial initialization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper introduces a Hessian-gradient alignment measure and margin estimation technique, comparing minima reached through normal, adversarial, large-norm, or wide-margin initialization; it does not reproduce the original magnitude-aware sharpness measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization changes the learned boundary and reported Gθ. On checkerboard the wide-margin solution generalizes better although Gθ is similar; on hierarchical gaussian the normal versus large-norm distinction is ambiguous due to variability.

fits_no_version.finding: Gθ generally distinguishes normally initialized solutions from adversarially initialized solutions described as worse-generalizing, but normal-versus-large-norm hierarchical-gaussian values overlap substantially.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a fixed architecture and dataset, the fraction of Hessian eigenvectors aligned with training gradients can indicate local decision-boundary complexity, with limitations.

fits_no_version.finding: Checkerboard narrow- and wide-margin solutions have similar Gθ values, while the authors describe the wide-margin solution as better-generalizing; their separate margin estimator distinguishes the boundaries.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Decision-boundary simplicity alone can miss generalization differences associated with margin width.

fits_no_version.finding: Unscaled Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue often rank the authors' worse-generalizing solutions as flatter; rescaling can change the Hessian spectrum while preserving predictions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unscaled Hessian curvature is not a reliable generalization proxy across these initializations and reparameterizations.

record.problems: The authors say the measure can miss boundary complexity far from training samples and can fail when simplicity bias hurts generalization. The checkerboard margin comparison shows Gθ nearly unchanged despite a generalization difference; normal versus large-norm initialization on hierarchical gaussian is ambiguous because the standard deviation exceeds the difference between means. The study uses small datasets and models, five runs for tabulated metrics, and acknowledges the need for more diverse datasets. It does not report direct numerical train-test gaps in the extracted measure comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Table 1 and Tables 2–3 report several additional metrics (trace(H), λmax(H), and parameter L2 norm); these are not separate rows because they are auxiliary comparison measures and do not test the magnitude-aware sharpness relation in V7.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy with matched architectures and recipes; chance-level random-label test accuracy. Random-label pretraining is only an initialization procedure here.
Test-error behavior as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out error, local connectivity, learned sparsity and transferred initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets. Appendix F compares gradient alignment and decision boundaries rather than held-out performance.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on held-out error across training-set sizes, dropout strengths and augmentation settings.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with measured train–test gaps, and its ranking against the specified norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Remove all V7 verdicts. A limitation of Gθ is not a limitation of magnitude-aware sharpness. The row states here indicate inability to determine a listed version's effect, not incorrect transcription of the tabulated Gθ values.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of fixed random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test-error behavior as width increases.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer generalization comparisons.
Large versus small batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
The study does not test magnitude-scaled weight perturbation sharpness or compare against the specific norm- and margin-based measures in the version.
Removing examples selected by memorization influence and comparing with random removals.

rows.operation_detail: Compared Gθ, Hessian trace, maximum Hessian eigenvalue, and parameter L2 norm across initialization procedures on gaussian; values averaged over 5 runs.
rows.note: Lower Gθ is interpreted by the authors as a simpler boundary and better generalization; the table compares Gθ alongside trace(H), λmax(H), and ||θ*||2. No explicit numerical train-test gap is given.
rows.check: Gθ is the authors' alignment-based measure, not magnitude-aware sharpness; its value cannot establish V7. This is proposed-method evaluation. Model size is approximately 10^5 parameters, not 105.
